title: I’m playing Super Mario Galaxy on my Android phone. Here’s how to get it on yours right now

body: Emulation isn’t new, and neither is running Nintendo games on smartphone hardware. Nintendo’s portable-first console experiences translate beautifully to smartphone hardware, making its platform a prime target for emulation. However, as good as emulation is, a native port always hits differently due to the performance improvements and reduced latency that it brings. Earlier this week, I came across a project dubbed Galaxy Android that brings Super Mario Galaxy, widely considered one of the greatest 3D platformers ever created, to Android as a native experience. Released as part of the OpenPort Labs project, the Android build makes copious use of AI to get it up and running, but it’s important to acknowledge the seven and a half years of effort by the Petari decompilation project to write the code by hand. With that in mind, the only real question was to see how well it performed.

body: TL;DR Tech researchers have developed a forensic tool that recovers deleted conversations from AI apps running locally on Android devices. In one experiment, the tool recovered 26 previously shared facts, compared with just 14 accessible to the original AI session. The technique requires forensic access to device data and doesn’t establish that conversations from cloud-based chatbots are similarly recoverable. Recovering deleted information from phones is hardly a new trick. We’ve seen it with text messages , photos, and other supposedly erased data. But researchers have taken things somewhere more intriguing: they’ve developed a forensic tool that can retrieve deleted AI conversations and actually bring the chatbot back to life, complete with some of its previous knowledge. According to researchers at Georgia Tech (via Digital Trends ), the technique uses a forensic tool called ORISA to piece together information AI apps leave behind on Android phones. title: YouTube streams may look better and buffer less as soon as early 2027
summary: AV2 is coming to YouTube in the not too distant future.
body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR YouTube has announced that it plans to roll out AV2 to the platform in early 2027. The AV2 codec will initially launch for the web version of YouTube. The company also hints at benefits for multi-view experiences. Earlier this year, the Alliance for Open Media released the definitive specs for the AV2 codec , which is expected to be about 25% to 32% more efficient than AV1. That means you get higher-quality streaming for the same bitrate or comparable quality at a lower bitrate. The benefit is that the codec can reduce the amount of bandwidth you’re consuming. YouTube is expected to adopt AV2, and it could arrive sooner than you would expect. While partners like Netflix, Amazon, and Apple have been quiet on rollout plans, it appears that YouTube isn’t quite as shy. According to FlatpanelsHD , YouTube has revealed that it is looking to roll out the codec in early 2027. The plan is to initially launch AV2 for the web version of the platform.
